prompt_free_text:
This paper addresses an important and underexplored mismatch between standard motion forecasting benchmarks and real deployment: in practice, forecasting is performed continuously over time rather than independently on isolated scene crops. The paper proposes RealMotion, which augments a standard encoder-decoder predictor with two temporal mechanisms operating across successive sub-scenes: a scene context stream that propagates scene-level context forward in time, and an agent trajectory stream that relays prior predictions through a memory bank to refine current forecasts. The paper also introduces a data reorganization procedure that converts benchmark scenes into short continuous sequences by splitting trajectories into multiple temporally ordered sub-scenes. Empirically, the method reports strong results on Argoverse 2 single-agent and multi-agent leaderboards and competitive results on Argoverse 1, together with ablations and an efficiency discussion.

Overall, I find the paper interesting and potentially impactful. The central premise is compelling: most forecasting methods indeed ignore the temporal continuity between successive forecasting calls, and this is a real limitation if the goal is deployment in autonomous driving stacks. The paper’s framing around “continuous driving” is therefore valuable, and the attempt to bridge benchmark structure and online inference is timely. The empirical gains, especially over the authors’ independent baseline and on Argoverse 2 leaderboard metrics, are substantial enough to suggest that the idea is not merely cosmetic. The method is also relatively lightweight in parameter count, which strengthens the practical angle.

That said, I also have several concerns regarding novelty clarity, experimental fairness, and methodological specification. These issues do not negate the contribution, but they currently prevent me from fully assessing how much of the gain comes from the proposed temporal modeling versus changes in supervision, data construction, and evaluation protocol.

The strongest aspect of the paper is the problem formulation. Recasting motion forecasting as a sequential inference problem is sensible and, in my view, more realistic than the dominant one-shot benchmark setting. The paper clearly articulates why historical scene context and prior predictions may help, including occlusion recovery and temporal consistency. This is a meaningful conceptual contribution even beyond the specific architecture. The data reorganization strategy is also practically useful, since it allows existing datasets to be repurposed for this setting without collecting new data.

The architecture itself is intuitive. The scene context stream propagates encoded scene features across time after alignment, while the trajectory stream uses a memory bank of prior predicted trajectories and mode features to refine current outputs. This decomposition into context propagation and trajectory relaying is reasonable and easy to understand. I also appreciate that the authors did not overcomplicate the base encoder-decoder and instead focused the novelty on temporal extensions. The ablations indicate that both streams contribute, and the latency table suggests the online version remains practical.

However, the paper currently underspecifies several important details. The data reorganization procedure is central to the contribution, yet it is described somewhat loosely. It is not fully clear how split points are chosen across datasets, how many sub-scenes are generated per original sample, whether all agents are guaranteed to exist across all sub-scenes, how map crops are defined and aligned, and whether future labels for earlier sub-scenes overlap heavily with later sub-scenes. Because the method trains on multiple overlapping sub-scenes derived from the same original trajectory, there is a risk that some of the gains come from denser supervision or easier intermediate prediction targets rather than from temporal reasoning per se. The paper partially addresses this with the RealMotion-I baseline, but that baseline is trained on the original independent data rather than on reorganized data without temporal state. Table 4 includes a “continuous data only” row, which is helpful, but more care is needed to isolate the effects of additional training samples, overlapping labels, and recurrent state propagation.

Relatedly, the comparison to prior work on official leaderboards is not entirely clean from a scientific standpoint. RealMotion is evaluated in a modified sequential setting during training and apparently also uses multiple iterative predictions at inference, while prior methods are trained and evaluated in the standard one-shot setting. Although the final benchmark submission may still produce one prediction per official sample, the training signal and inference context differ. This is not necessarily unfair, but it should be discussed more explicitly. In particular, the paper should clarify whether the model, at test time on Argoverse 2, has access only to the official observation window for the evaluated sample, or whether it effectively reconstructs preceding sub-scenes from the same sample and uses them as additional context. If the latter, then the method is exploiting information that standard methods do not use, even if it is technically derivable from the same raw sample. That is acceptable if clearly stated, but the paper should be more transparent about this distinction.

A major concern is whether the proposed setting truly matches real online deployment. In a real system, successive forecasting calls occur on a stream of sensor observations over time, with new observations arriving causally. In this paper, continuous sequences are retrospectively generated by splitting a fixed benchmark sample. This is a clever workaround, but it is not equivalent to a true streaming benchmark. The same original scene may provide a relatively clean and consistent temporal window, and the model may benefit from repeated exposure to overlapping history/future segments that are not representative of online distribution shifts, tracking noise, or scene entry/exit dynamics. The paper acknowledges some limitations, but I think this gap should be emphasized more strongly. The contribution is best interpreted as a benchmark adaptation plus temporal forecasting architecture, not yet a definitive solution to streaming motion forecasting.

On the methodological side, some design choices feel heuristic and insufficiently justified. For example, the scene context stream uses map-to-map and agent-to-scene cross-attention, but not agent-to-agent or map-to-agent temporal propagation in a more symmetric way. The rationale is plausible but not deeply argued. The trajectory stream stores predicted trajectories rather than latent states and refines current predictions via attention over trajectory embeddings. This is interesting, but it raises questions about error accumulation and confirmation bias: if earlier predictions are wrong, why does relaying them help rather than hurt? The paper suggests that similarity-based attention and refinement mitigate this, but stronger analysis would help. For instance, it would be useful to report performance as a function of memory bank size, prediction horizon, or prediction quality of stored trajectories, and to compare against using ground-truth historical futures during training only as an oracle upper bound. Similarly, the FIFO memory policy and the decision not to filter modes are asserted rather than justified.

The alignment mechanism is another area where more precision is needed. Equation (1) uses motion-aware layer normalization with relative pose and time encoding, but this is not a geometric transformation of features in the usual sense. For trajectories, Equation (3) applies an explicit Euclidean transform, which is clearer. For scene features, however, it is not obvious that MLN is sufficient to align map and agent features across local coordinate systems, especially when the visible map crop changes over time. The ablation shows some benefit from alignment modules, but the paper should explain more concretely what is being aligned and why this operation is appropriate. As written, “projecting” historical scene features onto the current system sounds stronger than what the module actually does.

The empirical results are promising, but some claims are overstated. The abstract and conclusion repeatedly claim state of the art, yet on Argoverse 2 the method is not best on all key metrics; QCNet remains slightly better on minFDE6, and ProphNet is better on b-minFDE6. The paper does mention “almost top 2” elsewhere, but the broader wording should be toned down. More importantly, the strongest gains are on single-mode metrics, especially minFDE1 and minADE1. This suggests the method may be particularly good at sharpening the top prediction rather than improving multimodal coverage. That is still valuable, but it should be analyzed. The paper briefly notes this pattern, yet does not investigate whether the trajectory stream reduces diversity or overcommits to a dominant mode. Since continuous forecasting should ideally improve both consistency and calibrated multimodality, additional analysis of mode probabilities, diversity, and calibration would strengthen the work.

The efficiency discussion is directionally useful but not fully convincing. The online/offline distinction is important, and I appreciate that the authors report both. However, the latency comparison mixes numbers from different sources and possibly different implementations. It is unclear whether all methods were benchmarked under identical preprocessing, hardware, and software conditions, or whether some numbers are quoted from prior papers. Also, the statement that offline latency for RealMotion is roughly three times online latency because only the final prediction is used for evaluation is intuitive, but it would be better to report exact end-to-end timing details, including preprocessing and memory updates. Since efficiency is a key claimed advantage, this section should be more rigorous.

The ablation section is useful but could be stronger. The component ablations support the value of continuous data, scene context, and trajectory relaying. Still, several critical controls are missing. First, compare against a baseline trained on reorganized continuous data but evaluated only on the final segment without recurrent state, to isolate whether the gain comes from curriculum-like supervision. Second, compare against simply concatenating longer history into the base model, since the reorganized setting may effectively expose more temporal context. Third, compare the trajectory memory bank against a simpler temporal smoothing baseline, such as averaging or Kalman-like refinement of predicted endpoints, to show that the learned relaying mechanism is necessary. Fourth, compare against storing latent scene states only, latent trajectory states only, and both, to better justify the two-stream decomposition.

I also think the paper should engage more directly with the closest prior work on streaming or temporal forecasting. The related work mentions one “pioneering work” on a temporal motion benchmark, but the distinction from that line of work is not deeply developed. Given that the main novelty is the continuous setting, the paper should more carefully position itself relative to prior streaming formulations, recurrent forecasting, and online prediction systems. As written, the novelty may appear larger than it is because the comparison is mostly against one-shot predictors.

There are also some presentation issues. The writing is generally understandable, but there are many grammatical errors and awkward phrasings that obscure technical points. Several claims are repetitive. Some notation is introduced imprecisely; for example, the indexing in Equation (3) and the meaning of q are not fully clear, and the dimensions of memory-bank tensors in Equation (4) are omitted. The paper would benefit from a careful proofreading pass and a more explicit algorithm box describing training and inference over a sequence of sub-scenes.

Despite these concerns, I do think the paper has real merit. The idea of exploiting continuity across forecasting calls is important, and the reported gains suggest that this direction is fruitful. The method is also reasonably simple and practical, which increases its potential impact. My main hesitation is that the current experimental setup conflates three things: a new problem formulation, a data transformation that changes supervision structure, and a temporal architecture. The paper needs to disentangle these more convincingly and be more explicit about what is and is not comparable to standard benchmark methods.

To strengthen the paper, I would recommend the following concrete revisions. First, clarify the exact train/test protocol under data reorganization, including what context is available at inference for benchmark submissions. Second, add stronger controls isolating the effect of reorganized supervision from recurrent temporal modeling. Third, provide more analysis of error accumulation and robustness in the trajectory memory bank, including memory size and quality sensitivity. Fourth, expand discussion of multimodality and calibration, since gains are concentrated in top-1 metrics. Fifth, improve the efficiency section with standardized timing methodology. Sixth, better position the work relative to prior streaming forecasting literature and tone down broad state-of-the-art claims where the method is not uniformly best.

In summary, this is a strong and interesting paper with a valuable practical perspective and promising empirical results. Its main contribution is less about a radically new forecasting architecture and more about reframing motion forecasting as a continuous process and showing that temporal state propagation across successive scenes helps. I am positive on the overall direction and think the paper could be impactful, but I would like to see clearer protocol transparency and stronger controls before fully endorsing the claims. My overall assessment is moderately positive.

prompt_structured_json.summary: The paper proposes RealMotion, a motion forecasting framework for continuous driving that departs from the standard independent-scene formulation. The method reorganizes benchmark scenes into temporally ordered sub-scenes, then uses two recurrent temporal modules: a scene context stream that propagates historical scene features via cross-attention, and an agent trajectory stream that stores past predicted trajectories/features in a memory bank and refines current predictions using trajectory-conditioned attention. Experiments on Argoverse 1/2 single-agent and Argoverse 2 multi-agent benchmarks report strong leaderboard performance and favorable latency/parameter counts relative to selected baselines.
strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored mismatch between benchmark evaluation and real deployment: forecasting is repeatedly invoked over time rather than once per isolated scene.
The proposed formulation is intuitively meaningful: leveraging prior scene context and prior predictions could improve temporal consistency and exploit information from earlier observations.
The architecture is modular, with a clear decomposition into scene-context propagation and trajectory-memory refinement.
Empirical results are strong on Argoverse 2 single-agent test metrics, including notable gains over QCNet on minFDE1/minADE1 and competitive results on other metrics.
Includes ablations on major components, alignment modules, trajectory embedding, split points, gradient steps, and attention depth.
Efficiency discussion is useful; the reported parameter count is small and online latency is competitive.
The paper openly discusses limitations of the data reorganization strategy and benchmark constraints.
weaknesses: The central experimental claim is confounded by the custom data reorganization: RealMotion is not evaluated under the same input protocol as most compared methods, so improvements may partly stem from additional effective temporal context rather than the proposed modeling alone.

The paper lacks a rigorous definition of the continuous-driving task and evaluation protocol. It remains unclear exactly what information is available at each sub-scene, how overlap between segments is handled, and whether the protocol preserves fairness with standard benchmark settings.

Method description is underspecified in several places: memory bank retrieval policy, number of stored trajectories actually used, whether gradients flow through time across segments, how mode correspondence is maintained across timestamps, and how multi-agent predictions are formed from a primarily single-agent description.
Comparisons to prior streaming/temporal forecasting work are limited. The paper cites streaming motion forecasting but does not provide direct empirical comparison or careful differentiation.
Some claims are overstated, e.g., 'far outperformed most previous approaches' despite mixed results across metrics and the fact that QCNet remains best on minFDE6.

The qualitative evidence is weak: only a small number of examples are described, and there is no systematic analysis of cases where temporal context helps (e.g., occlusion, intent disambiguation, interaction-heavy scenes).
Writing clarity is uneven, with grammatical issues and ambiguous terminology that make technical details difficult to verify.
methodological_flaws: Potential fairness issue in empirical comparison: the proposed data reorganization effectively creates sequential sub-scenes and may expose additional usable context compared with standard one-shot baselines. Since most baselines are reported from leaderboards under the original protocol, the comparison is not an apples-to-apples test of modeling quality.

Possible train/test protocol mismatch: the paper reports 'offline' evaluation requiring three iterations and only using the final prediction, while also emphasizing 'online' deployment. It is unclear whether the benchmark test submission exactly matches the claimed continuous setting or whether gains partly arise from repeated refinement unavailable to standard methods.

Equation (3) is mathematically unclear/incomplete. The transformation of trajectories uses y_i^{ori}=y_i[Δt·q], but indexing by Δt·q may be non-integer or out of range depending on memory age; the paper does not specify interpolation, clipping, or validity conditions. The rotation/translation convention is also ambiguous.

The scene-context alignment via MLN is not a geometric projection of features; it is a learned conditioning mechanism. Claiming that it 'projects' historical scene features into the current coordinate system is scientifically imprecise and may overstate what the operation guarantees.

The trajectory-memory refinement may introduce exposure bias/error accumulation because it relays past predictions rather than ground truth during inference, yet the paper does not analyze robustness to incorrect memory contents or compounding errors.

Ablations do not isolate the contribution of the recurrent modeling from the increased supervision/data augmentation effect of splitting scenes into multiple segments. ID-2 already improves substantially with only reorganized data, suggesting part of the gain may come from altered training distribution rather than continuous reasoning.

Efficiency comparison is not fully controlled: latency numbers compare online/offline variants across methods with different caching assumptions and possibly different implementations/hardware optimizations, so conclusions about practical efficiency are suggestive rather than definitive.

The multi-agent evaluation is insufficiently justified methodologically. The paper states it lacks specialized multi-agent design, but does not explain how joint consistency across agents is enforced or how the sequential memory interacts across multiple agents, limiting confidence in the scientific interpretation of those results.
